items.headline: Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire Extended 45 Days; Second-Front Compound-Risk Removed Through ~July 1; No Day-1 Project Freedom Resumption Order; Trump Sends New Iran Nuclear Proposal
items.summary: Three developments dominate Saturday morning's geopolitical picture. First and most consequential: the United States confirmed on May 15-16 that Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 45-day ceasefire extension following two days of Washington talks. The extension was announced by the US State Department on May 15, with CNBC, Bloomberg, and CGTN confirming as of May 16. The second-front compound-risk trigger that was flagged as the highest-priority secondary watch item in every brief since May 12 — the May 17 ceasefire expiry coinciding with the post-summit IRGC window opening — is now removed from the 24-48 hour risk register. The extension runs approximately to July 1. Follow-on talks are scheduled for June 2-3 in Washington. Critical caveat: Al Jazeera reports that Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon have continued despite the extension — the ceasefire has 'never been observed in practice,' with 657+ Lebanese deaths since it began. The structural disarmament impasse (Hezbollah arms retention) remains unresolved; the extension buys time without solving the underlying architecture. Second: no Project Freedom resumption order was issued in the first 24 hours following Trump's departure from Beijing on May 15. The May 15-18 window was flagged in yesterday's brief as the highest-risk resumption period of the cycle; passing Day 1 without an order incrementally reduces but does not eliminate imminent-resumption probability. CENTCOM repositioning, White House War Powers notification, and Trump Truth Social Iran statements remain the top watch items. Third: overnight, Trump sent Iran a new nuclear proposal — the Wall Street Journal characterizes this as a 'fresh bid' with a warning that swift progress is necessary to avoid serious consequences. This follows Trump's May 11 'totally unacceptable' rejection of Iran's counteroffer. The new proposal signals that the deal track, while near-terminal, has not been formally abandoned by the administration. The Iranian parliamentary hardliners' dominant posture ('war reparations, full Hormuz sovereignty, end sanctions') has not shifted. The IRGC cyber window is fully open with no inhibiting factor remaining.

items.headline: Markets Sell Off Day 1 of Warsh Era: S&P Loses 7,500; 10-Year at 4.55%; Rate-Hike Odds at 45%; Warsh Policy Compression Acute on Day 2
items.summary: The May 15 market session — the first trading day of Kevin Warsh's Federal Reserve Chair era — ended in a broad equity selloff driven by Treasury yield pressure from the hot inflation prints. The S&P 500 fell 1.24% to 7,408.17, erasing the 7,500 level that had been recaptured Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost approximately 537 points. The 10-year Treasury yield spiked nine basis points to 4.55%, its highest level in approximately a year. The 30-year bond yield moved above 5%. The 2-year yield tested 4.00%. The yield curve steepening signals that markets are pricing an extended period of elevated rates driven by supply-shock inflation that is immune to rate tools. CME FedWatch as of Friday close: probability of at least one rate hike by year-end 2026 jumped to 45% — up from approximately 21-25% mid-week and from effectively 1% one month ago. This is the most dramatic repricing of Fed policy expectations since the Hormuz crisis began. The April CPI (released May 13) confirmed at +3.8% year-over-year (three-year high, up from 3.3% in March), core +2.8%; combined with the April PPI (+1.4% monthly, +6.0% annual) released May 15, the wholesale-to-retail transmission of Hormuz energy-price pressure is confirmed accelerating. Warsh's policy dilemma is acute: the inflation driver (Hormuz supply disruption) is immune to rate-tool intervention; rate hikes risk compressing growth while not reopening the Strait; rate cuts risk amplifying price pressure; and Trump's public rate-cut pressure is explicit and unretracted. Warsh's first FOMC meeting is June 16-17 (31 days away). No Warsh inaugural public statement on rate posture has been confirmed released as of Saturday morning; any statement this weekend will be the primary market-moving signal of the day. A Brent crude price last confirmed near $104 (down from May 11's $107.77 peak) provides minor relief at the margin.

items.headline: Senate Finance Deadline Missed; June 1 Reconciliation Target at Structural Risk; DHS $72B Package Advancing Separately
items.summary: The Senate Finance Committee's May 15 submission deadline for Reconciliation 2.0 provisions to the Budget Committee passed Friday without confirmed text release as of Saturday morning. This is the first concrete structural evidence that Trump's June 1 reconciliation completion target is at risk — a milestone flagged as the key watch item in every brief since May 11. The Finance miss is particularly significant because the committee's tax and revenue provisions represent the most complex and politically contentious component of any budget reconciliation package. Without a Finance submission, the Budget Committee cannot begin markup, and the Byrd Rule review and CBO scoring process cannot be initiated. Senate leadership has not confirmed a revised timeline or a request for a deadline extension as of this morning. The June 1 target — publicly committed to by President Trump and Senate Majority Leader Thune — now faces its first operational test of structural viability. Separately, the narrower DHS/defense-focused Reconciliation 2.0 package is advancing on a parallel track: the $72B package (appropriating ICE/CBP funding through 2028, increasing defense spending by $1.2T over a decade) was released by Senate committees on May 4-7 and is proceeding independently of the Finance text. This two-track structure may reflect an administration decision to decouple the more straightforward DHS enforcement funding from the contested revenue provisions, potentially allowing a partial reconciliation advance before the Finance text is ready.
